extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and patent applicants (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining claim limitations that exclude subject matter (negative limitations), focusing on definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and written-description support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre‑AIA 112. Covers when negative language is permissible, required disclosure support, and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of negative limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The current view of the courts is that there is nothing inherently ambiguous or uncertain about a negative limitation; so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely, albeit negatively, the claim complies with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations are not per se indefinite. The examiner/ drafter should evaluate whether the negative wording nonetheless sets clear boundaries for the claim scope. Older case law criticized certain negative limitations, but modern precedent accepts negative limitations that define clear boundaries. See examples and cases cited (In re Schechter, In re Wakefield, In re Barr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming by exclusion (indefiniteness risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative limitation that attempts to claim the invention by excluding what the inventors did not invent (i.e., defining the invention primarily in terms of what it is not) can render the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for phrasing that effectively claims by exclusion rather than describing the invention. Example of problematic language: 'R is an alkenyl radical other than 2‑butenyl and 2,4‑pentadienyl' (In re Schechter) — held to be indefinite because it attempted to claim by excluding unclaimed matter. Where the negative limitation simply excludes a few known alternatives that are clearly defined in the disclosure, it may be acceptable; where it merely says 'other than' undefined or numerous alternatives, risk of indefiniteness increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness requirement applied to each recited negative limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each recited limitation — including negative limitations — must itself be definite. If the negative limitation is definite, the claim may be allowable despite being phrased negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the definiteness of each negative phrase individually. Example: the limitation 'said homopolymer being free from the proteins, soaps, resins, and sugars present in natural Hevea rubber' was considered definite because each referred characteristic was definite (In re Wakefield). Similarly, 'incapable of forming a dye with said oxidized developing agent' was held definite where the boundaries were clear (In re Barr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations must have basis in the original disclosure (written description support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any negative limitation or exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure; without such basis, the negative limitation fails the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification positively recites alternative elements, those alternatives may be explicitly excluded in the claims (In re Johnson; Ex parte Grasselli). The examiner should look for explicit support in the original filing for excluding specific elements or features. If the negative limitation is not supported by the specification, the claim should be rejected under the written description requirement; see MPEP § 2163–§ 2163.07(b) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive recitation of alternatives permits later exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification describes alternative features or elements positively, the applicant may later exclude those alternatives in the claims via negative limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support can be inferential where the specification describes 'the whole' such that it 'necessarily described the part remaining' — court authority (In re Johnson) supports that a description of alternatives can provide basis to exclude particular alternatives. Ex parte Grasselli and related authority confirm that explicit positive disclosure of alternatives is a sound basis for exclusion in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant need not articulate advantages/disadvantages to exclude alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is not required to explain the advantages or disadvantages of alternative features in the specification in order to later exclude those alternatives in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has held that describing alternative features without discussing pros/cons does not preclude later excluding options in claims (Inphi Corp. v. Netlist, Inc.). Drafting practice: you do not need to describe why an excluded alternative is inferior to have support for excluding it, but you must still have sufficient disclosure to show possession of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere silence in the specification generally does not provide basis for a negative limitation (but may in special circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere absence of a positive recitation in the specification is not generally sufficient to support a negative claim limitation; silence will not generally suffice to support a negative claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where the disclosure would reasonably convey to a person skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter, a negative limitation may be supported even without explicit positive recitation. Ex parte Parks noted lack of literal basis may not establish a prima facie lack of descriptive support. Novartis Pharms. Corp. v. Accord Healthcare, Inc. (quoting Ariad) emphasizes that the disclosure must 'reasonably convey[] to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.' Consider whether a skilled artisan would understand from context that the negative limitation is necessarily present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) where negative limitation lacks written‑description basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim containing a negative limitation which does not have basis in the original disclosure should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph) for failing to comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining or drafting, if you cannot identify adequate support in the original disclosure for a negative limitation, apply a written description rejection. Cross‑reference MPEP §2163–§2163.07(b) for detailed written‑description analysis and examples. Document why the claimed exclusion is unsupported and provide references to the specification (or lack thereof).
